cards.title: Vulnerability-Based Trust Definition
cards.summary: Trust on a team means confidence that peers' intentions are good, so people admit weaknesses and mistakes without fear of reprisal.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why your ops, marketing and supply-chain leads won't surface problems (stockouts, bad creative, missed launches) until it is too late to fix them.
steps: Define trust for your team in behavioral terms rather than as a feeling: the confidence that peers' intentions are good and that admitting a weakness or mistake will not be punished.
Tell the team explicitly, as the source's leader does, that a store that hides its dirty laundry (botched launch, high return rate caused by a bad PDP, an out-of-stock hero SKU) cannot fix it.
Model it first: admit your own mistake or skill gap in front of the group, since the source treats leaders' vulnerability as the trigger for everyone else's.

Watch for the observable tell that trust is absent — no debate in meetings where people clearly disagree in private, and calm, unobjectionable discussion. Use that silence as your diagnostic, not as a sign of alignment.

Give the team a low-stakes on-ramp such as personal-history questions before pushing work-critical admissions; the source notes light disclosure warms people quickly but the effect fades once work issues arise.
caveats: The source is a business fable plus a model section, not a controlled study; treat the claims as the author's framework.
Personal-history exercises produced a warm glow that faded once work resumed; they open the door, they don't build the trust.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Distinguish Ideological Conflict from Personal Fighting
cards.summary: Productive conflict argues about concepts and ideas to reach the best answer fast; destructive conflict attacks people and makes teams avoid debate altogether.
cards.use_when: Run product-range, pricing or campaign-planning reviews where disagreements either produce a sharper plan or turn into politics that people avoid.
steps: Frame the purpose of the debate before it starts: the objective is the best answer for the store, not winning or protecting anyone's function.
Require participants to attack the idea (the assortment, the price point, the creative angle, the promotion mechanic) and never the person who proposed it.

Make absence of visible debate a red flag, not a sign that things are fine. The source's leader treats a meeting where nobody disagrees as evidence of a hidden problem when the team is known to disagree privately.

If someone keeps an unspoken objection (eyerolls, 'I don't know what you're talking about', passive resistance), have a peer or the leader surface it in the moment rather than smoothing it over, because the source deliberately lets a peer challenge the behavior.
Allow emotional heat during the exchange and don't rush in to make artificial peace; the source's leader resists rescuing participants.
caveats: Silence can genuinely mean alignment when everyone is truly on the same page — the source concedes this hypothetical, so treat silence as a prompt to check, not proof.
Conflict requires the trust of good intentions first; running this without that foundation produces personal fighting.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Five Dysfunctions Model as a Diagnostic Triangle
cards.summary: The model stacks absent trust, fear of conflict, lack of commitment, avoidance of accountability and inattention to results, with trust as the base.
cards.use_when: Diagnose why launches slip, decisions get re-litigated, or nobody owns a metric, so you can sequence fixes instead of attacking symptoms.
steps: Draw the model as a triangle with four horizontal bands, five sections, trust at the bottom, and use it as a shared language with the team.

Score the team's behavior against each layer in order: do people admit mistakes (trust), do they disagree openly (conflict), do they commit to a decision once it is made (commitment), do they hold each other to it (accountability), and does the group focus on store results rather than individual wins (results)?
Treat the layers as ordered: if the bottom layer is weak, work there first, because the upper layers are functions of it.
Say out loud that the model is simple on paper and hard to practice — the source's own framing — so the team doesn't dismiss it as obvious.
Use the diagnosis to set the agenda of a dedicated off-site rather than trying to fix the layers in ordinary working meetings.
caveats: This is the author's consulting framework, not a validated instrument; the source itself acknowledges the fiction and does not present research evidence.
Teams may show symptoms at several layers at once; the ordering is a sequencing heuristic, not a strict dependency proof.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: First Real Discipline: Publicly Narrow the Team's Job to Results
cards.summary: The leader states up front that the off-site and the team exist for one reason only — achieving results — and that some people may not fit the new company.
cards.use_when: Kick off a turnaround or restructuring of how merchandising, marketing and supply chain leads operate together, when resistance to time out of the office is high.
steps: Open by naming the gap between resources and outcomes rather than the people: more experienced staff, more cash, better tech, stronger board, yet behind competitors on revenue and growth.
State the single purpose plainly: everything you do as a group is about making the business succeed, and results are the only true measure of a team.

Name the likely consequences honestly: changes are coming and some people may decide this is not the place for them. The source frames this as realistic probability, explicitly not a threat and not aimed at an individual.
Defuse the 'touchy-feely' objection in advance — clarify that no one is catching anyone falling out of trees or holding hands; this is about performance, not bonding.
Point at the concrete measures the team will judge itself by, such as revenue growth, profitability, customer retention and satisfaction, rather than abstract team health.
caveats: Telling a team members may leave is a high-stakes move; the source presents it as a leader who already has the board's backing and a specific turnaround mandate.
Do not use this language as a bluff or to single someone out — the source explicitly denies targeting anyone.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Observe First, Change Second
cards.summary: A new leader spends the first weeks walking the floor, sitting in meetings and taking notes before making any structural change.
cards.use_when: Take over an ecommerce team (or a new function such as retention or marketplace ops) and need a diagnosis before reorganizing roles or processes.
steps: Interview each direct report and sit in as many existing meetings as possible as a silent observer, taking notes rather than intervening.
Keep the existing meeting leader in place temporarily if it lets you observe norms rather than perform authority; the source's leader leaves the former CEO running staff meetings for two weeks.
Walk the floor and talk to front-line staff — for a store, that means support tickets, warehouse staff and merchandisers, not just department heads.
Do not accept incoming agenda suggestions for your diagnostic session; hold your own agenda so the discussion stays on the problems you came to assess.
Expect backlash for spending visible time on diagnosis; the source shows the board and peers questioning the leader's inactivity before she has produced anything, and she holds the line.
caveats: Works when you have explicit backing and enough time to observe; without that, the same behavior reads as passivity.
The source is a fable and the two-week window is illustrative, not a recommended duration for any particular situation.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Handle Moments of Truth Face-to-Face, Not by Email
cards.summary: When someone breaks an agreed priority, address it in person immediately and hold the priority, offering help instead of relenting.
cards.use_when: A key team member wants to skip a planning session, launch review or pricing meeting for a customer or vendor meeting that conflicts.
steps: Resist replying by email; go to the person directly, as the source's leader does when her technologist books a sales trip over the retreat.
Acknowledge the opportunity sincerely before delivering the ruling, so the discussion is about priorities rather than about the person.
Restate the one priority that currently outranks everything: getting the team working together, because without it there is nothing to sell.
Offer concrete help with the reschedule and any leverage you have, such as a relationship with the counterparty, rather than just denying the request.
Expect pushback to reach you later through other channels — a peer, a board member — and hold the line consistently rather than being surprised by it.
caveats: Only credible if you actually have one clearly stated priority; the source's leader does.
Treating every customer meeting as subordinate to internal work is a judgment call, not a universal rule — the source presents it as correct because the team was the bottleneck.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Defend the Off-Site Investment Against 'Real Work' Objections
cards.summary: Multi-day off-sites are justified when the team's dysfunction is the actual bottleneck, and the leader must absorb the criticism for taking people out of the office.
cards.use_when: Decide whether to pull merchandising, paid media and supply-chain leads out of trading for a planning reset.
steps: Choose a location close enough to avoid expensive travel but far enough to slow people down; the source uses a modest inn rather than a distant resort.
Pick an off-season, reasonably priced venue with one comfortable, private conference room so the group has nowhere else to go.
Schedule for early arrival and full days, and expect teammates to test the commitment — the source has one participant arrive at 8:59 for a 9:00 start.
Tell the team plainly that you know the time out of the office feels unreasonable and that they will understand by the end why it matters.
Plan breaks (the source gives a whole free afternoon) and expect a long evening session, so energy is spent where the real work happens rather than in a single exhausting block.
Reject incoming topic suggestions when they don't serve the diagnosis; the source's leader refuses a peer's proposed agenda item because she has her own.
caveats: Justification depends on dysfunction actually being the constraint; if the store's issue is a broken funnel or an out-of-stock crisis, time away has a higher opportunity cost.
The source's leader had board support and a turnaround mandate; without that, sustained criticism may block the work.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Set Two Simple Ground Rules: Be Present, Participate
cards.summary: The leader's only meeting rules are that everyone is fully engaged, off-topic items are flagged openly, and laptops stay closed.
cards.use_when: Run weekly trading, range-review or campaign-planning meetings where people are half-attending and decisions stall.
steps: State the two rules directly: be present and participate in whatever the group is discussing.

Create an explicit carve-out: if a topic only concerns two people and is wasting the group's time, anyone may say so and take it offline. This gives the objection a legitimate channel instead of silent disengagement.
Ban open laptops in discussion meetings and give the reasoning — people assume the user is checking email — while allowing notebooks.
Distinguish the behavior from the technology or culture: the source's leader points out the same laptop problem existed in manufacturing and the issue is behavioral, not industry-specific.
Expect a challenge on the laptop rule from someone invoking company culture; answer calmly and let the room see the rule is about attention, then let the person comply without an ultimatum.
caveats: A hard laptop ban may be impractical for roles on call for live incidents; the source presents it as a discussion-meeting rule, not an all-day policy.
The carve-out can be abused to dodge hard topics; the source frames it as for genuinely off-topic items only.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Personal Histories Icebreaker with a Hard Boundary
cards.summary: A 45-minute exercise of five mild personal questions makes a team noticeably more at ease, but the effect fades once work pressure returns.
cards.use_when: Open an off-site or a first cross-functional planning session where the group is guarded toward each other.
steps: Choose five low-risk, non-clinical questions such as hometown, number of siblings, interesting childhood hobbies, biggest challenge growing up, and first job.
Draw the boundary explicitly so no one fears over-disclosure: you want their childhood, not their inner child.
Run it round-robin with everyone answering, including the leader, so status differences flatten; the source notes the leader's surprising answer (a college sports honor) changed how the team saw her.
Expect a visible lift — the source describes teammates as tighter after roughly 45 minutes than at any time in the previous year.
Plan for the lift to decay once the group turns to work. Use the exercise as a door-opener, then immediately move into substantive work while people are still loose.
caveats: The source explicitly notes the euphoria diminishes when the conversation shifts to work, so don't count it as trust-building by itself.
In the source, one member (Mikey) stayed outside the exchange and became the object of no teasing at all — visible non-participation is itself a signal worth noting.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Use Personality Instruments as Self-Disclosure, Not Assessment
cards.summary: Have the team complete diagnostics like Myers-Briggs beforehand and review them together, because people enjoy talking about themselves and it legitimizes differences.
cards.use_when: Reduce friction between, say, a data-driven growth lead and an intuition-led brand lead before a joint planning cycle.
steps: Have each member complete the instrument before the session, not during it, so meeting time goes to discussion.

Review results together and focus on implications for how the group works: who needs time to think, who speaks first, who needs detail. The source discusses introvert/extrovert differences explicitly.
Expect high engagement during the self-description phase; the source notes even the most disengaged member participated.

Anticipate that the mood changes once criticism begins — the source says people like learning about themselves until the criticism comes, so schedule the harder feedback work for when you have time and energy.
Use the shared vocabulary for light, good-natured ribbing afterward as evidence it landed, since teammates in the source tease each other about being too meticulous or too unfocused.
caveats: The source does not validate the instruments and one member dismisses the whole exercise as psychobabble; expect resistance and decide in advance how much to push.
Personality talk can become an excuse for behavior ('that's just how I am') if not tied back to results.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Let the Group, Not Only the Leader, Confront Behavioral Problems
cards.summary: Peer challenge lands harder than leader intervention; the leader should resist making artificial peace and let an eyeroll or a barb get named in the room.
cards.use_when: A long-standing behavior (cynicism in reviews, passive-aggressive objections, chronic lateness) is souring a cross-functional team.
steps: Identify the specific recurring behavior rather than the personality — the source's example is eyerolling when a colleague disagrees about marketing.
When it happens in a session, pause and let a peer ask directly what the look or remark meant instead of the leader rescuing either party.
If the person denies the behavior, let another colleague (the source uses a peer known for gentleness) describe how it lands and offer a face-saving way to admit it.
Resist the urge to smooth things over when the exchange gets sharp; the source's leader eats her pizza and watches, consciously not making artificial peace.
Note what the confrontation costs the room — the source flags the beer at dinner as a bad idea — and adjust the setting next time so people aren't primed to spar.
caveats: The source's own tension is that the leader wanted to protect the person being sniped at and chose not to; this is a judgment call about timing, not a rule to let conflict run unchecked.
Denial is a common response; escalation without a private follow-up can leave the person publicly cornered.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Protect the Team's Weak Link and Low-Maintenance Contributors
cards.summary: The leader should quietly build relationships with struggling members and lean on reliable generalists who absorb unglamorous work.
cards.use_when: Allocate your management attention across a team where some roles are ill-defined and some people are visibly disengaged.
steps: Read individual behavior in context rather than as fixed character: the source's leader reasons that a distracting teammate is probably unaware of how she comes across, since no one would act that way on purpose.
Decide whether the person is relieved rather than resentful of a demotion or role change; if relieved, keep them on your team and tell them to participate fully.
Identify one low-maintenance, trustworthy member who takes on quality and other unattractive duties, and be explicit that this frees your attention for the harder problems.

Note when a member's role has not fully developed — the source's COO had the most ill-defined role on the team, and the source presents that ambiguity as a live risk even when the person doesn't complain.
Watch for quiet superiority: one member privately deemed colleagues inferior while building shallow relationships. Treat superficially smooth relationships as a signal to probe, not reassurance.
caveats: The source's judgments of individuals are narrative setups in a fable, not validated assessments.
Tolerating an ill-defined role indefinitely carries risk; the source leaves it as an unresolved problem at this point in the story.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Sequence Rewards and Rhythms Around Collective Results
cards.summary: Shift rewards from individual performance metrics toward collective achievements and run a fixed meeting rhythm anchored on team results.
cards.use_when: Design incentives and the operating cadence for a merchandising, growth or supply-chain group whose members optimize their own metrics and never a joint outcome.
steps: Audit current incentives for individual-only measures (personal GMV, personal ROAS, personal open-to-buy) and identify where they reward behavior that harms the whole, such as one channel bidding up costs for another.
Move weight toward collective achievements tied to store-level outcomes, so individual targets do not compete with the shared result.
Establish a fixed meeting rhythm: a multi-day off-site at least once, weekly staff meetings, and ad hoc topical meetings for issues that don't fit the standing agenda.
Keep weekly staff meetings bounded (the source uses roughly two hours) so they function as a decision cadence rather than an open-ended update.
Tie the cadence back to results, since the source names results as the only true measure of a team.
caveats: The source states the shift in reward systems as a recommendation with no data on outcomes; treat it as a design direction, not a proven incentive plan.
The specific meeting durations (two-day off-site, two hours weekly) come from one company's setup and may not transfer.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx
